# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-10 13:01 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 179 active entries of tips_notebook.json (20 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier sheets are in history/.

## Everyone
- A visit shows a destination, not an action: tracks and watches can't tell protection from framing or a Katana hit. A corroborated Lookout's lone other visitor to a victim is near-proof; don't let the 'Lookout can't see himself' caveat acquit a repeat visitor. (seen in 12 games)
- Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting. A read/vote mismatch is a lead to check against claims and results, never a reason to hang or shoot alone. (seen in 10 games)
- Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results. Remember a contradiction alone doesn't separate a Yakuza from a Jester who wants the hang. (seen in 10 games)
- Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once. (seen in 9 games)
- Write each night's planned target and all results into your will, labelled as plans, so your death still yields information. (seen in 7 games)

## Village
- Map early PM clusters and co-nominations; a group that DMs then pushes together is a likely bloc. Require votes or a mechanical result before hanging on a PM link, since Jesters and Executioners also leave PM trails. (seen in 14 games)
- After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them. A Guilty vote clears no one. (seen in 12 games)
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises far above awkward wording. Before a hang, ask what separates a lie from a mistake, a frame, a Roleplayer or a Jester. (seen in 12 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. While a Ritualist may live, never name a living player's exact role in public or in your will. (seen in 12 games)
- Keep Serial Killers and Arsonists in the pool after Yakuza die; a Not Evil read or Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and a failed kill can mean innate Defense. (seen in 8 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack or is blocked night after night is likely real. (seen in 8 games)
- Investigators and Medics: never announce tonight's target publicly or by PM; it tells the Pharmacist whom to block and the Katana where to strike. (seen in 6 games)
- Once an archive or survey list is public, do slot math daily; a claim that duplicates a once-listed role or overflows unseen slots marks a liar. (seen in 5 games)
- If an announced trial total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists among the voters on the larger side; pick them out by stance/ballot mismatch. (seen in 4 games)
- If the nominee may be a Jester, prefer not hanging; if you must, agree on a bare Guilty majority and keep confirmed power roles off the Guilty side. (seen in 4 games)

## Yakuza
- Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty. But first do the vote math in night chat: if your Innocents (plus a doubled vote) can save them, defend them. Futile lone Innocents hang you later. (seen in 15 games)
- Fake-claim only a role whose token count matches yours and that no living holder, Lookout or Tracker can contradict; never report more results than its tokens allow. (seen in 11 games)
- Never put team plans in daytime PMs and don't PM teammates on Day 1; Eavesdroppers and Wiretaps read them, and PM triangles become the town's case. (seen in 10 games)
- After a failed Katana, assume protection or innate Defense: kill or block the protector, or hang the survivor, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 9 games)
- Give the Katana to a low-value member with a cover story ready, and move it the same night a Lookout or Tracker names the holder. (seen in 7 games)
- Every member submits the agreed holder, target and actions every night; with two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 6 games)
- Never flatly deny a visit that could have been seen; agree a cover action in night chat and admit it at once. (seen in 5 games)
- Spend one-shot tokens (rig, puppet, clean) on a decisive day; a dead Yakuza's unused token is wasted. (seen in 4 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged. (seen in 3 games)

## Sheriff
- Post every target and result in your first speech after getting it, and counterclaim at once with your full log if someone copies your role. (seen in 8 games)
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result clears nothing; say so when posting, and in the endgame rely on votes instead. (seen in 13 games)

## Medic
- Protect likely Katana targets, analysts then claimed investigators. Once you've claimed Medic, self-protect with a token instead of repeating a predictable protection. (seen in 11 games)
- You get no save feedback; say the target's survival is consistent with your protection, never that you confirmed a save. (seen in 4 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, Evil check against an unverifiable claim, flipped teammate's links), never a soft read; a hidden Cardinal costs two Good lives. Use Basic shots. (seen in 6 games)

## Clerk
- Rig on a set night for a non-teammate who can pass a nomination but not a Guilty vote; never when a teammate is the likely nominee, and don't hoard it. (seen in 4 games)

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3+ living players are doused or the moment you're suspected; Arsonists who kept dousing were hanged with no kills. (seen in 3 games)

title: Post-game lessons: tips players wish they'd known, and how past tips went

task:
If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

You were also given tips from past games (in your instructions). Which of them went especially well or badly for you or others this game? List only tips that clearly mattered (or none): helped, hurt (followed it and it backfired, or it was predictable to opponents), or wrong (it is false or contradicts the rules), and why, concretely.

lessons.tip: Survey groups that include the player whose alignment or role you most need; my N2 survey of Erin/Frank/Grace found a Clerk, but the group was too wide to tell which of three was Yakuza, so pick groups of tighter suspicion or pair it with votes.
Withholding a checkable night result for two Days cost credibility and forced repeated pressure; state the role and the exact result on the first Day, even if it is only exact-role information.

Treat a census or survey that names a group but not which member is the target as weak evidence on its own; verify a claim by comparing it with votes, visits and private-message traces before hanging.

Watch who opposes testing a lead while later voting Innocent on the same suspect; a player who rejects a trial and then hangs with the group may be coordinating, so ask for their reasoning before a vote.
Do not let a geometry or rules objection drive a nomination without checking it yourself; Dave's skip-rule error pushed a Good Surveyor to trial and cost him credibility.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results.

lessons.tip: If you hold a token-based power role, use it on Night 1 when the outcome is safe. A Katana kill on Night 1 wastes the role's tokens and effects entirely. A Prosecutor who prosecutes at night still gets the prosecution even if they die that night (R21), so act before a likely night kill.

Before accepting or rejecting a claim about a group (Surveyor, Census Taker, Diviner), count the circle yourself. Start from the living order at the start of the night, skip the user, and list the neighbours. Two players this game disputed a legal group for a full day and were wrong.

Withholding a result does not protect you. Yakuza kill on a schedule regardless, and a silent investigator takes suspicion while still dying. Give your exact result and its type (alignment, exact role, visit) in your first public speech.

Do not let the Clerk rig a Day where your own teammate is likely to be nominated. A rigged nomination executes the nominee whatever the vote, so a rig that Yakuza use on a Day when they are the nominee kills their own side.

On a rigged Day, a passed nomination is an execution. Treat any nomination you cannot verify as lethal and withhold Yes votes until you know whether a rig is active, since an announced Innocent verdict can still end in hanging.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's Day 2 trial was stopped when the claimed contradiction (the Surveyor geometry) was checked and found wrong, so the Village avoided a wrong hang.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi and Carol checked the skip-self rule and cleared Carol, after Dave and Erin had called her group impossible; this prevented an innocent execution.

tips_feedback.tip: Write each night's planned target and all results into your will, labelled as plans.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's and Frank's wills published their night results after death, which gave the Village concrete (if unverified) information to weigh.

tips_feedback.tip: Spend one-shot tokens (rig, puppet, clean) on a decisive day.
tips_feedback.why: Frank spent his Clerk rig on Night 2 for Day 3, and the Day 3 nominee was Frank himself. The rig executed its own user, which shows the Clerk tip's caveat about teammate nominees was not respected.

tips_feedback.tip: Every member submits the agreed holder, target and actions every night.
tips_feedback.why: Grace's Katana kills on Nights 1 to 3 went through each time because Frank and Grace matched their night submissions, which kept the Yakuza kill rate high.

lessons.tip: Before alleging a mechanical contradiction, rebuild the relevant player circle exactly as it stood when the action happened and apply special rules such as skipping the investigator. If challenged, check the calculation before voting; a mistaken accusation can damage your credibility and endanger a good player.

State precisely what a group result establishes. “One member of this group has role X” does not identify which member, and a census count does not identify who has which alignment until combined with independently confirmed facts. Treat a player's own claim as a claim, not corroboration.

Track nomination votes separately from trial votes. Opposing even a trial for a teammate is distinct evidence from voting Innocent once the trial begins; neither vote alone proves guilt, but the full record can reveal who tried to shield whom.

When you withhold a result, explain what kind of result it was and why you are holding it back. Give enough detail for others to evaluate its scope and mechanics without disclosing a future target; unexplained vagueness invites suspicion.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them. A Guilty vote clears no one.
tips_feedback.why: After Frank flipped Yakuza, Grace's No on his nomination was a useful lead: Bob had supported putting Frank on trial, while Grace had opposed testing him. Her Innocent vote was not independently informative here because the Clerk rig forced Frank's execution regardless of the verdict.

lessons.tip: Survey groups that include the player whose alignment or role you most need; my N2 survey of Erin/Frank/Grace found a Clerk, but the group was too wide to tell which of three was Yakuza, so pick groups of tighter suspicion or pair it with votes.
Withholding a checkable night result for two Days cost credibility and forced repeated pressure; state the role and the exact result on the first Day, even if it is only exact-role information.

Treat a census or survey that names a group but not which member is the target as weak evidence on its own; verify a claim by comparing it with votes, visits and private-message traces before hanging.

Watch who opposes testing a lead while later voting Innocent on the same suspect; a player who rejects a trial and then hangs with the group may be coordinating, so ask for their reasoning before a vote.
Do not let a geometry or rules objection drive a nomination without checking it yourself; Dave's skip-rule error pushed a Good Surveyor to trial and cost him credibility.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results.
tips_feedback.why: I refused to hang Frank on the census alone on Day 3 and kept the Carol trial from becoming a hang on a withdrawn geometry error.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep Serial Killers and Arsonists in the pool after Yakuza die.
tips_feedback.why: Not applicable here; no such roles appeared, so the tip did not affect the outcome.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't hint at your power role on Day 1.
tips_feedback.why: I withheld my Surveyor result for two Days, which made Village treat me as suspicious and gave the Yakuza a reason to push the trial on me.

lessons.applies_to: Everyone, especially Surveyors and anyone evaluating a Surveyor claim
lessons.tip: Work out the group from the target by walking the living circle in both directions, skipping the Surveyor if encountered and continuing until you find the nearest eligible players. Check the current circle carefully before calling a group impossible.

Choose someone likely to send or receive Day private messages who is likely to survive the night. Eavesdropping reveals messages during the following Day, not Night chat, and a target who dies before that Day gives you nothing to read.

Separate nomination votes from trial verdicts. An Innocent vote may be shared by many players, but a No vote that prevents testing a confirmed Yakuza can be a useful lead—still weigh it against that player's stated reasoning and the rest of the vote record.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once.
tips_feedback.why: Dave's Surveyor-geometry objection was wrong, but the other players checked the circle and corrected it before the trial verdict. Carol was found Innocent rather than being hanged on a false mechanical claim.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them. A Guilty vote clears no one.
tips_feedback.why: After Frank flipped as Yakuza, Grace's No vote on his nomination stood out: Bob also voted Innocent at trial, but Bob had supported putting Frank on trial. Grace was then scrutinized and flipped as the other Yakuza.

tips_feedback.tip: Write each night's planned target and all results into your will, labelled as plans, so your death still yields information.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's will preserved her Surveyor results after she died, including the group containing Frank and the Clerk result. That information remained available for evaluating claims and votes.

lessons.tip: Treat group results as constraints, not accusations. Keep each possible assignment alive until another independent fact distinguishes them; a claimed alignment or role is not independent confirmation.
State the reason for your trial vote, especially if it differs from your public lean. An unexplained vote change makes even a correct vote harder for others to evaluate.

After a Yakuza flips, separate the vote to put them on trial from the verdict vote. Someone who opposed testing them is a more useful lead than someone who merely voted Innocent alongside several others.
Track tokens as submitted actions, not assumed successful transfers. In your will, distinguish what you attempted from what the recipient's later account or will actually confirms.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them. A Guilty vote clears no one.
tips_feedback.why: After Frank flipped as Yakuza, Grace stood out because she had voted No on his nomination, while Bob had supported putting him on trial before voting Innocent. That distinction helped the living identify Grace as the remaining Yakuza.

lessons.tip: A rig forces the execution of whoever is successfully nominated, even if the trial vote is Innocent. Before using it, account for who might be nominated—including yourself or a teammate—and save it for a day when the likely nominee is an opponent.

When a teammate is likely doomed, calculate whether your votes can actually save them. If not, consider supporting the nomination and Guilty vote to avoid leaving a distinctive defense pattern that surviving players can use after the flip.
Make your submitted actions match what you told your teammate in night chat. If you change your mind, say so clearly; otherwise your partner plans around an action that you will not actually take.
Plan one-shot abilities around the day they can change the outcome. If you may be eliminated, an unused token is lost; remember that puppeting controls chat, not the target's nominations or votes.

A night kill does not erase public results or a dead player's will. Plan for how the living will interpret the information after the claimant dies, rather than assuming removing the claimant removes the case.

tips_feedback.tip: Yakuza: Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty after checking the vote math.
tips_feedback.why: Grace did the opposite on Frank's trial: she voted No on his nomination and Innocent. After Frank flipped Yakuza, Bob used the distinctive No vote as a concrete reason to suspect Grace, who was then executed.

tips_feedback.tip: Clerk: Rig for a likely non-teammate nominee; do not rig when a teammate is likely to be nominated.
tips_feedback.why: Frank used the rig on a day when Heidi's census had already put pressure on him. The rig made his execution automatic despite an Innocent majority, so the effect killed its own user.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, scrutinize players who opposed the nomination or voted Innocent when those votes could have saved them.
tips_feedback.why: After Frank's flip, Bob distinguished Grace's No on the nomination from his own Yes, then used that difference to press her for an explanation. It helped the Village identify and execute the remaining Yakuza.

lessons.tip: Before a Katana kill, check whether the target is a likely Surveyor, Census Taker or other investigator. Their results name the Katana holder's visit, so a holder who visits and attacks repeatedly gets exposed by counter-visits. Rotate the holder or use a Clerk or Puppeteer swap on the investigator in the same night.

Do not let a teammate's public stance become the whole case. Frank's Yes-then-Innocent pattern and Grace's No on his nomination both became Village talking points. If a teammate is at risk, argue the vote math early and make your own stance look consistent with the town's read.

Night chat plans were fully visible to the town afterwards through the revealed record. Agree on a cover story for each Katana attack (for example a claimed visit) before the night, because any unexplained visit to a dead investigator will be checked.

A Census Taker or Surveyor result that names a group only proves a set of players, not a role. Treat 'exactly one of X and Y is Good' as a lead that cannot convict either person alone; the town hanged Frank and Grace on group-based reads that could not separate them from one another.

Late multi-round public pressure (repeated 'answer directly' demands) cost the town several rounds of budget and produced little. Ask one precise checkable question per turn and let the answer or silence speak.

tips_feedback.tip: Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty, but first do the vote math in night chat.
tips_feedback.why: Frank was not bussed by a Yes vote here; instead the town noticed Frank's Yes and Innocent swings on Carol and used them against him. The tip is not clearly wrong, but it did not hold because the vote math was not the decisive factor.

tips_feedback.tip: Never put team plans in daytime PMs and don't PM teammates on Day 1.
tips_feedback.why: We kept Day PMs minimal; Heidi's and Carol's PMs to Frank were visible, but none of our team plans were in them, so the town could not read our night plan from daytime chat.

tips_feedback.tip: Give the Katana to a low-value member with a cover story ready, and move it the same night a Lookout or Tracker names the holder.
tips_feedback.why: Grace held the Katana every night and was the holder through Day 4, and the Census Taker and Surveyor counted Good and visited patterns that tied the holder to the attacks. The tip was not followed in practice, and the predictable holder kept the town's focus on the Yakuza side.

lessons.applies_to: Census Taker and other alignment-count roles
lessons.tip: A census or survey counts true alignment, so a 2-of-3 Good result with a Neutral in the group does not identify a Yakuza. Before treating a count as proof, list every alignment the result allows, including Neutral, and check which group members can be cross-examined.

Before nominating on a geometric or group claim (survey skip rules, census groups), write out the legal groups step by step. Dave's wrong skip-rule nomination of a Good Surveyor cost him credibility and nearly hanged an innocent player.

A Clerk rig executes any successfully nominated player even when the trial vote is Innocent. Once a Clerk may be alive, treat every successful nomination as a possible death, and do not nominate someone you would not accept losing.

A publicly pressuring investigator who questions a suspect on Day 2 can be Katana-killed the next night. Post your results early and keep your will updated each night, so the town still gets your information if you die.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction.
tips_feedback.why: I checked Carol's skip-rule geometry myself, confirmed her group was legal, and that exposed Dave's wrong nomination instead of letting the town hang a Good Surveyor.

tips_feedback.tip: Write each night's planned target and all results into your will, labelled as plans.
tips_feedback.why: My will carried my Night 1 census result and the Good/Evil deduction, so the town received that information publicly when I died on Night 2.

summary: Village won 4-0 over the two Yakuza, Frank (Clerk) and Grace (Puppeteer). The key information came from Heidi's Night 1 census: Alice, Dave and Frank, 2 of 3 Good. Once Alice flipped Prosecutor and Dave claimed Eavesdropper, which Carol's survey supported, Frank was the obvious non-Good player. The Yakuza then killed Heidi on Night 2, so her flip and will confirmed the census. Carol's Night 2 survey added a Clerk among Erin, Frank and Grace. The decisive mistake was Frank's: in night chat he told Grace he would hold the Clerk rig, then rigged Day 3 anyway while he was the most likely nominee. Dave nominated Frank, the nomination passed 4-2, and the rig hanged him even though the trial went 3-3 Innocent. Grace had seen the Yakuza summary and knew about the rig. She still cast the only No on Frank's nomination besides Frank himself, and after Frank flipped Clerk that vote was the town's whole case against her. She killed Carol on Night 3, never used her puppet token, and was hanged 3-1 on Day 4. Village made errors of its own. Dave and Erin pushed a trial on Carol over a misread of the Surveyor skip rule. Carol withheld her result for three rounds and drew that suspicion on herself. Bob voted Innocent on Frank under a strict 'name a concrete contradiction' standard, which would have saved a Yakuza if Frank had not rigged his own hanging.

lessons.tip: Never rig a Day on which you or a teammate is the likely nominee: a rig executes anyone whose nomination passes, including Yakuza. Rig only when you are not under pressure and a Village target can win a nomination but not a Guilty vote. Tell your team truthfully what you are doing.
lessons.evidence: Frank told Grace he would hold the rig, then rigged Day 3 while Heidi's census pointed straight at him. His nomination passed 4-2 and the trial went 3-3 Innocent, but the rig hanged him anyway.

lessons.tip: When a teammate's nomination is clearly going to pass, or a rig makes passing fatal anyway, vote Yes and Guilty to bus them. A lone protective vote that changes nothing becomes the case against you once they flip.
lessons.evidence: Grace knew about the rig and still voted No on Frank's nomination, which passed 4-2 regardless. On Day 4, Bob, Dave and Erin all named that No vote as the reason to hang her.

lessons.tip: Combine partial results with flips and corroborated claims. A 'k of 3 Good' census becomes a named suspect once the other members are confirmed Good, so nominate and vote on it instead of waiting for a direct contradiction.
lessons.evidence: From Heidi's census plus Alice's Prosecutor flip and Dave's Eavesdropper claim (supported by Carol's survey), Dave correctly deduced Frank. Bob and Erin still treated the census as naming no one, and Bob voted Innocent on Frank.

lessons.tip: Before calling a result mechanically impossible, re-derive it from the rule text. For neighbor groups (Surveyor, Diviner), the user's own seat is skipped. A wrong 'impossible' call wastes a trial and costs the accuser credibility.
lessons.evidence: Dave and Erin called Carol's Bob/Dave/Erin survey group impossible and sent her to trial. The group was legal because Carol's own seat is skipped. Both had to retract, and Grace later used the error against Dave.

lessons.tip: Once you are asked directly, post your role, target and result promptly, ideally in your first speech after the result. Withholding them invites a trial and helps no one, because the Yakuza can't see the result anyway.
lessons.evidence: Carol hid her Surveyor result for three rounds, was nominated twice and put on trial, then admitted the delay was a mistake. Her result turned out to corroborate Dave.

lessons.tip: Killing the investigator whose public result already points at you lets the flip and the last will confirm that result. If the result is already damning, plan the Day around it instead: prepare a counter-narrative, bus, or use your Day tools.
lessons.evidence: Killing Heidi on Night 2 made her Census Taker flip and will confirm the census. Dave opened Day 3 by nominating Frank on exactly that basis.

lessons.tip: Spend Day-shaping tokens such as the puppet before the endgame. Taking over a key accuser's or swing voter's chat on a crucial Day can redirect a trial, while a token you die holding does nothing.
lessons.evidence: Grace died on Day 4 still holding her puppet token. She never puppeted Dave or Bob on Day 3 or Day 4, the Days that decided the game.

lessons.tip: Give your tokens to the token-limited investigator whose claim is best supported, and publicly claim the gift so their notification backs up your own claim.
lessons.evidence: Erin gave Carol two survey tokens. Carol's will confirmed receiving them, which cleared Erin on Day 4, and the extra tokens funded Carol's surveys.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them. A Guilty vote clears no one.
tips_feedback.why: After Frank flipped Clerk, Bob, Dave and Erin singled out Grace's No on his nomination, set it apart from Bob's Yes-then-Innocent, and hanged the last Yakuza on Day 4.

tips_feedback.tip: Rig on a set night for a non-teammate who can pass a nomination but not a Guilty vote; never when a teammate is the likely nominee, and don't hoard it.
tips_feedback.why: The tip was correct, and ignoring it decided the game. Frank rigged the Day he was the obvious nominee, and the rig hanged him despite an Innocent verdict.

tips_feedback.tip: Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty. But first do the vote math in night chat: if your Innocents (plus a doubled vote) can save them, defend them. Futile lone Innocents hang you later.
tips_feedback.why: The game proved it right. Grace knew about the rig and that Frank's nomination had 4 Yes votes, so her No was futile, and it was exactly what got her hanged.

tips_feedback.tip: Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once.
tips_feedback.why: Dave and Erin broke it by miscalculating the survey group and sending Carol to trial. Heidi and Bob followed it by re-checking the skip rule, which got Carol a unanimous Innocent verdict.

tips_feedback.tip: Write each night's planned target and all results into your will, labelled as plans, so your death still yields information.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi's will repeated her census, which gave Day 3's nomination of Frank its basis. Carol's will confirmed her Clerk survey and Erin's token gift.

tips_feedback.tip: Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results. Remember a contradiction alone doesn't separate a Yakuza from a Jester who wants the hang.
tips_feedback.why: Bob and Grace treated the census as naming no one and so not a contradiction. Bob voted Innocent on Frank, and the trial ended 3-3, which would have saved him without the rig. On Day 4 Grace leaned on this standard, demanding the town name a contradiction or vote Innocent.

tips_feedback.tip: Spend one-shot tokens (rig, puppet, clean) on a decisive day; a dead Yakuza's unused token is wasted.
tips_feedback.why: Frank spent his rig on the wrong Day, the one where he was the obvious nominee, so it hanged him. Grace went the other way: she held her puppet token until her death, so it did nothing.

issues.description: Night 2: Frank (Clerk) explicitly agreed in Yakuza chat to take no Clerk action ('I'll take no Clerk action tonight; let's preserve the rig'), and Grace confirmed 'no Clerk rig'. Yet the recorded night action shows Frank spending his clerk token to rig Day 3, and the moderator processed it. The rig then caused Frank's own execution on an Innocent verdict (3 of 6 Guilty). Either Frank submitted an action that contradicts his own stated plan, or the harness parsed his earlier proposal as the action. The contradiction should be checked.

Frank's Yakuza chat referred to 'I'll save the puppet token for now' as if it were his own, but the puppet token belongs to Grace (Puppeteer). This is minor confusion about which teammate holds which role or token.

Day 2: Dave, then Erin, called Carol's Surveyor group (Bob, Dave, Erin) mechanically impossible because they forgot the Surveyor's skip-yourself rule. Surveying Dave skips Carol, so the neighbors are Bob and Erin. Dave nominated Carol on this basis; the first nomination failed, and Erin's second nomination passed and put her on trial before both withdrew the claim. This misreading of the circle/skip rules drove a wasted trial.

Day 2: Erin and Frank asserted that 'Alice dying doesn't itself erase a night result' for Dave's Eavesdropper action. In fact the Eavesdropper's whole effect is reading the target's private messages the following Day, so a dead target yields nothing. This is minor confusion about how the Eavesdropper role works.
